title: Obscure, but not meaningless
source_text: Εἰκὸς μὲν οὖν εἶναι λόγους πολλῷ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἕξεως σοφωτέρους, τοὺς δυναμένους ἀποδεικνύναι ψευδόμενον ἐν τούτοις τὸν Κέλσον καὶ ἐνθέους τὰς προφητείας· πλὴν καὶ ἡμεῖς κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν πεποιήκαμεν, τὰ, ὥς φησι Κέλσος, πάροιστρα καὶ πάντῃ ἄδηλα πρὸς λέξιν διηγησάμενοι ἐν τοῖς πραγματευθεῖσιν ἡμῖν εἰς τὸν Ἡσαΐαν καὶ εἰς τὸν Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ εἴς τινας τῶν δώδεκα. θεοῦ δὲ διδόντος τὴν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ προκοπὴν καθ᾿ οὓς βούλεται χρόνους προστεθήσεται τοῖς ἤδη εἰς ταῦτα ὑπαγορευθεῖσιν ἤτοι τὰ λείποντα ἢ ὅσα γ᾿ ἂν φθάσωμεν σαφηνίσαι. καὶ ἄλλοι δὲ οἱ βουλόμενοι ἐξετάζειν τὴν γραφὴν νοῦν ἔχοντες τὸ γνῶμα αὐτῆς εὑρεῖν ἂν δύναιντο, οὔσης ἀληθῶς πολλαχοῦ ἀσαφοῦς μὲν, οὐ μὴν. ὥς φησι Κέλσος, τὸ μηδέν. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ δύναταί τις ἀνόητος ἢ γόης ἐξομαλίσαι ἢ ὅπῃ ποτὲ τὸ λεχθὲν σφετερίσασθαι· μόνος δὲ καὶ πᾶς ὁ κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν ἐν Χριστῷ σοφὸς τὸν εἱρμὸν πάντα ἀποδῴη ἂν τῶν μετ᾿ ἐπικρύψεως εἰρημένων ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, „πνευματικα πνευματικοῖς“ συγκρίνων καὶ κατασκευάζων ἀπὸ τῆς συνηθείας τῶν γραφῶν ἕκαστον τῶν εὑρισκομένων. οὐ πιστευτέον δὲ τῷ Κέλσῳ λέγοντι τοιούτων ἀνθρώπων γεγονέναι αὐτήκοον. οὐδὲ γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς Κέλσου χρόνους γεγόνασί τινες π (ροφῆται) τοῖς ἀρχαίοις παραπλήσιοι, ἐπεὶ κἂν παραπλησίως τοῖς πάλαι γρ (αφεῖ) σιν ἀνεγράφησαν καὶ ἑξῆς προφητεῖαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποδεξαμένων καὶ θαυμασάντων αὐτάς. δοκεῖ δέ μοι πάντῃ δῆλον εἶναι τὸ τοῦ Κέλσου ψεῦδος, ὅτι οἱ δῆθεν προφῆται, ὧν αὐτήκοος ἐγένετο, ἐλεγχθέντες ὑπὸ Κέλσου ὡμολόγησαν αὐτῷ οὗ τινος ἐδέοντο, καὶ ὅτι ἐπλάσσοντο λέγοντες ἀλλοπρόσαλλα. ἔδει δ᾿ αὐτὸν καὶ ὀνόματα θεῖναι ὧν ἔφασκεν αὐτήκοος γεγονέναι· ἵνα ἐκ τῶν ὀνομάτων, εἴπερ εἶχεν εἰπεῖν, φανῇ τοῖς κρίνειν δυναμένοις, πότερον ἀληθῆ ἢ ψευδῆ ἔλεγεν.
pass_a_gloss: It is likely, then, that there are words (λόγος) much wiser than our condition (ἕξις), able to show Celsus lying (ψεύδομαι) in these things and the prophecies inspired (ἔνθεος); yet we too have done according to what is possible to us, having explained (διηγέομαι) word for word (πρὸς λέξιν) the things, as Celsus says, [Celsus:] 'frenzied (πάροιστρος) and wholly unclear (ἄδηλος)', in the works treated (πραγματεύομαι) by us on Isaiah and on Ezekiel and on some of the Twelve. And God granting (δίδωμι) the progress (προκοπή) in his word, at the times he wishes, there will be added to the things already dictated (ὑπαγορεύω) on these either the things lacking (λείπω) or as many as we may get ahead to make clear (σαφηνίζω). And others too who wish to examine (ἐξετάζω) the Scripture (γραφή), having mind (νοῦς), could find its sense (γνῶμα), it being truly in many places unclear (ἀσαφής), yet not, as Celsus says, [Celsus:] 'nothing'. But neither can any senseless man (ἀνόητος) or sorcerer (γόης) level it out (ἐξομαλίζω) or appropriate (σφετερίζομαι) what was said in any direction; but alone, and every one, the one truly wise in Christ could render (ἀποδίδωμι) the whole train (εἱρμός) of the things said with concealment (ἐπίκρυψις) in the prophets, [quotation] 'comparing (συγκρίνω) spiritual things with spiritual' and establishing (κατασκευάζω) each of the things found from the usage (συνήθεια) of the Scriptures. Celsus must not be believed saying he became an ear-witness (αὐτήκοος) of such men. For neither in Celsus's times were there any p(rophets) similar to the ancient ones, since [otherwise] prophecies would have been written up (ἀναγράφω) in sequence (ἑξῆς), like the writ(ing)s of old, by those who accepted (ἀποδέχομαι) and admired (θαυμάζω) them. It seems to me that Celsus's lie (ψεῦδος) is wholly clear, that the so-called (δῆθεν) prophets, of whom he became an ear-witness, being refuted (ἐλέγχω) by Celsus, confessed (ὁμολογέω) to him what they wanted (δέομαι), and that they were fabricating (πλάσσομαι) saying shifting things (ἀλλοπρόσαλλος). He ought also to have put names of those he claimed to have heard; so that from the names, if he had [them] to say, it might appear (φαίνομαι) to those able to judge (κρίνω) whether he spoke true or false.
pass_b_english: It is likely, then, that there are arguments far wiser than our ability allows, which could show that Celsus is lying here and that the prophecies are inspired. Still, we too have done what we could: in the works we have composed on Isaiah, on Ezekiel and on some of the Twelve, we have explained word by word the passages that Celsus calls “frenzied and altogether obscure.” And if God grants progress in his word, at the times he wills, there will be added to what we have already dictated on these books either what is still lacking or as much as we manage to make clear.

Others too, who wish to examine Scripture and have sense, would be able to find its meaning. It is truly unclear in many places, but it is not, as Celsus says, “nothing.” Nor can any fool or sorcerer smooth it out, or make what was said his own in whatever way he likes. Only the one who is truly wise in Christ, and every such person, could set out the whole connected sense of what was spoken with concealment in the prophets, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:13) and establishing each thing he finds from the usage of the Scriptures.

We must not believe Celsus when he says that he heard such men with his own ears. For in Celsus’s time there were no prophets like those of old; otherwise their prophecies too would have been written down one after another by those who accepted and admired them, as were the writings of long ago. And Celsus’s lie seems to me wholly plain from his claim that these supposed prophets whom he heard in person, when Celsus refuted them, admitted to him what they were after, and that they had been making it up, saying things that meant now one thing, now another. He ought also to have given the names of those he claimed to have heard in person, so that from the names, if he had any to give, it might be clear to those able to judge whether he was telling the truth or lying.

choices.choice: Single words and phrases of Celsus repeated from 7.9 (‘frenzied and altogether obscure’, ‘nothing’) are in double quotation marks. The report that the false prophets confessed to Celsus when he refuted them is Origen’s indirect account of a claim in Celsus’s text and is left unquoted. Copy-text restorations: π(ροφῆται) and γρ(αφεῖ)σιν are Koetschau’s supplements and are translated as ‘prophets’ and ‘writings’; the stray stop in οὐ μήν. ὥς φησι is ignored. 1 Corinthians 2:13 (πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες) is quoted with the word order reversed. ‘The Twelve’ are the Minor Prophets; Origen refers to his own commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel and some of the Twelve. ἐξομαλίσαι (‘level, smooth out’) rendered ‘smooth it out’. ἀλλοπρόσαλλα (‘now this way, now that’; Homer’s epithet for Ares) rendered ‘things that meant now one thing, now another’. μόνος δὲ καὶ πᾶς rendered ‘Only the one ..., and every such person’. ἕξις rendered ‘ability’. σφετερίσασθαι rendered ‘make ... his own’, matching the English of Celsus’s sentence in 7.9.
ἢ ὅπῃ ποτὲ τὸ λεχθὲν σφετερίσασθαι: 'or make what was said his own in whatever way he likes', matching the revised Celsus quotation in 7.9 and 7.10
1 Corinthians 2:13 checked (πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες, order reversed by Origen)
